user_query: Mitigating hallucination in LLM-based scientific literature review
answer_text: Hallucination remains the central obstacle to trustworthy LLM-based literature reviews: models generate plausible but fabricated claims and citations. A recent survey frames mitigation from a capability-enhancement perspective and identifies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as the most consistently effective strategy (arXiv:2510.24476). Grounding generation in retrieved sources and verifying citations against them is especially critical for scientific reviews, where fabricated references directly undermine credibility (arXiv:2604.01461). Architecture and data quality matter as well: fine-tuning on curated domain corpora and diversifying training data measurably reduce hallucination rates (arXiv:2512.02527). Verification-style pipelines such as Chain-of-Verification and claim-level self-checks further cut unsupported statements before they reach the reader. Overall, the literature converges on combining retrieval grounding with post-hoc citation verification as the practical recipe for reliable automated reviews.

user_query: Evaluating RAG systems with LLM-as-a-judge frameworks
answer_text: Evaluation of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems has shifted from manual inspection to automated LLM-as-a-judge pipelines. RAGAS is the leading open-source framework, scoring faithfulness, answer relevancy, and context precision/recall by prompting an LLM judge directly (arXiv:2309.15217). ARES takes a different route: it fine-tunes lightweight judge models on synthetic data and applies prediction-powered inference to produce statistical confidence intervals (arXiv:2311.09476). The broader LLM-as-a-judge paradigm was popularized by MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, which showed strong agreement between GPT-4 judges and human preference (arXiv:2306.05685). Practitioner guides emphasize the 'RAG Triad' - context relevance, groundedness, and answer relevance - as the minimal evaluation surface. Open challenges remain around judge bias, position effects, and aligning automatic scores with expert human judgments.

user_query: Defending autonomous LLM agents against indirect prompt injection
answer_text: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) - malicious instructions riding inside tool outputs - is the primary attack surface of autonomous LLM agents. Recent defenses cluster into a few families. Instruction-detection approaches train or prompt a detector to spot injected instructions before they reach the agent (arXiv:2505.06311). Architectural approaches isolate the agent from untrusted content: AgentVisor virtualizes the agent's execution environment to contain both direct and indirect injections (arXiv:2604.24118). A 2026 evaluation argues that out-of-band strategies - checking tool results through a separate channel - are converging as the most robust option for tool-using agents (arXiv:2606.26479). Test-time defenses such as Task Shield enforce task alignment so the agent ignores instructions that deviate from the user's goal (ACL 2025). Practitioners also combine spotlighting and delimiting of tool results with least-privilege tool permissions. Reported results show that prompt-based defenses alone still suffer high attack success rates, which motivates hybrid architectural designs.

user_query: Multi-agent collaboration for complex reasoning tasks in LangGraph
answer_text: Multi-agent systems built on LLMs coordinate specialized agents to tackle tasks that a single model struggles with, such as multi-step reasoning and tool orchestration. A 2025 survey systematizes collaboration mechanisms - cooperative debate, role assignment, and orchestration topologies - across LLM-based multi-agent systems (arXiv:2501.06322). In practice, frameworks like LangGraph represent agent workflows as graphs, giving precise control over message passing and shared state; the LangGraph+CrewAI report shows graph-structured orchestration improving information flow while CrewAI contributes role-based task allocation (arXiv:2411.18241). Work on synergizing logical reasoning with knowledge management reports that agent teams outperform single-agent baselines on reasoning-heavy benchmarks (arXiv:2507.02170). LangGraph's official guidance recommends dividing complicated problems into tractable units handled by specialized agents under a supervisor. Open challenges include benchmarking multi-agent conversations and the cost of redundant inter-agent communication.

user_query: Self-correction and reflection mechanisms in Agentic AI
answer_text: Self-correction and reflection are core mechanisms of agentic AI: the agent critiques its own outputs and retries with adjusted plans. Reflexion established the pattern - the agent verbalizes reflective feedback from failed trials into episodic memory, improving later attempts without weight updates (arXiv:2303.11366). An empirical study finds that LLM agents using self-reflection can identify and correct their own mistakes when given error signals, though gains vary by task (arXiv:2405.06682). Surveys of agentic LLMs formalize reflection as an external algorithm that assesses predictions and re-prompts the model for self-correction (arXiv:2503.23037). Recent work on self-improving systems splits the field into foundation-model improvement versus scaffolding-level reflection, including GUI agents trained via iterative online reflection tuning (arXiv:2607.13104). Notably, recent surveys also document negative results: self-correction without external feedback can degrade performance, which motivates verifier-grounded reflection loops.
